title: Toilets don’t flush the opposite way south of the equator
body: Earth’s spin nudges anything moving across its surface: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern. Over hundreds of kilometres and many hours, that steers whole weather systems, so lows spin anticlockwise in the north and clockwise in the south. In a toilet or sink the nudge is negligible: the bowl’s shape and the way the water came in matter far more. Only a carefully settled basin, like Ascher Shapiro’s in 1962, shows the effect.

slides.alt: Animation: on a weather-map globe, a northern storm spins anticlockwise and a southern one clockwise. Air flowing into a low bends right; circles show Earth’s spin needs 100 km for wind and 1 km for slow water, against a half-metre sink. Two toilets swirl alike, and a settled basin turns.

slides.heading: How Earth’s spin sets a storm turning

steps.label: Air rushes in toward a low-pressure centre
North of the equator it bends to the right
The inflow curls into an anticlockwise spin
It only shows in huge, long-lived systems

slides.heading: Shapiro’s basin
slides.text: In 1962 at MIT, Ascher Shapiro used a basin about 2 m across, with a small wooden cross over the plug, and let the water settle for at least 24 hours. Draining took 20 minutes; the cross began turning only after about 15, anticlockwise.

slides.label: the Coriolis acceleration, as a share of gravity
slides.text: That tiny push is why Shapiro’s test needed extreme precision. Tests in Sydney later saw clockwise turning.

slides.question: Why doesn’t the Coriolis effect decide which way your sink drains?
options: It only acts on salt water
It cancels out at most latitudes
It is far too weak at that small scale
Sinks drain too fast for any force
slides.explanation: The Coriolis effect only matters over large distances and long times. In a bowl, its shape and the way the water entered are likely to be far stronger.

slides.heading: Which one is not steered by the Coriolis effect?
slides.explanation: Hurricanes, ocean currents and shells flying for kilometres move far enough for Earth’s spin to bend their paths. A bathtub is far too small for the effect to matter.
